title: The lilac chaser
hook: Stare at a ring of lilac dots and they vanish, replaced by one racing green dot.
peek: A ring of twelve fuzzy lilac dots blinks out one at a time around a cross. Fix your eyes on the cross for a few seconds and the lilac dots disappear completely, leaving a single green dot that seems to chase itself round and round.
lede: The picture is simple: twelve blurry lilac dots arranged in a circle around a small black cross, with one dot briefly disappearing in turn so the gap travels around the ring. Look at the moving gap and that is all you see. Keep your eyes on the cross for a few seconds, though, and the lilac fades away and a green dot appears, running in circles.

bullets.text: The illusion was created by Jeremy Hinton around 2005 and spread widely after the vision scientist Michael Bach put it on his website of optical illusions. It quickly became one of the most shared illusions online.

The green dot is not on the screen at all. Each gap leaves a brief negative afterimage, and the opposite of lilac is a pale green. As the gap jumps along, your brain links those afterimages into one moving dot.

The lilac dots vanish because they are soft-edged and sit away from where you are looking. When the eyes stay still, the visual system gradually stops reporting blurry, unchanging things in the corner of vision, so they fade into the grey background.

The chaser stacks three effects: the afterimage supplies the colour, Troxler fading removes the real dots, and the same apparent motion that makes cinema work turns a series of jumps into one smooth run.
